groups.content:
The Antikythera mechanism

Discovery

  • 1900: Greek divers sheltered near Antikythera because of a [1]

The mechanism

  • 1902: identified when an archaeologist saw a [3] wheel inside a lump of bronze
  • at least 30 bronze gears, originally kept in a wooden [4]
  • covered with writing in [5] that explained how it worked

Questions 32-36

In boxes 32-36 on your answer sheet, write

YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writers
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writers

Questions 37-40

Complete the summary using the list of words, A-G, below.

Write the correct letter, A-G, in boxes 37-40 on your answer sheet.

A   competition
B   foundations
C   funding
D   coincidence
E   accidents
F   inspiration
G   rewards
groups.content:
Where do new ideas come from?

The popular view is that a major discovery is the result of a sudden moment of [37] in the mind of one brilliant person. In fact, the same discovery is often made by different people at around the same time. This is not a matter of pure [38]; rather, it happens because every invention is built on the [39] provided by earlier work. [40] may also play a part, as Fleming's discovery of penicillin shows, but only when the scientist is ready to recognise its importance.

questions.explanation: Answer: storm Paragraph 1: the divers 'were forced by a storm to take shelter near Antikythera'.
Answer: bodies Paragraph 1: Stadiatis claimed 'he had seen a heap of dead bodies '.
Answer: gear Paragraph 2: Stais 'noticed that one of them contained a gear wheel'.
Answer: box Paragraph 2: the gears 'were once housed in a wooden box '.
Answer: Greek Paragraph 5: the surfaces 'were covered with thousands of tiny Greek letters, forming a kind of instruction manual'.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The government supported the recovery, but the passage says nothing about paying the divers.
Answer: FALSE The work was dangerous: ' one diver died and two others were left paralysed '.
Answer: TRUE The ship sank around 70-60 BCE, but ' the mechanism itself may be considerably older ', perhaps from around 200 BCE.
Answer: TRUE ' By turning a handle on its side, the user could set it to any date '.
Answer: FALSE ' Nothing of comparable complexity is known to have existed for more than a thousand years afterwards '.
Answer: FALSE 'Even so, much of the text remained hidden inside the corroded fragments '.
Answer: TRUE ' around two-thirds of the original mechanism is missing '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage only says nobody knows whether further dives will find more pieces; it does not say whether any dives are planned.
Answer: C Section C: the deep roots of intermediate wheatgrass reach water, ' so it continues to grow well through long periods without rain '.
Answer: B Section B: ' But growing annuals comes at a cost. ' Soil is washed or blown away, and fertiliser pollutes rivers.
Answer: E Section E: ' Breeders are now working on perennial versions of other crops, including sorghum, sunflowers and chickpeas. '
Answer: A Section A: early farmers took ' thousands of years '; breeders today are trying to do something similar 'in a matter of decades'.
Answer: C Section C: Marsh expected health food, ' but it actually has a lovely sweet, nutty flavour '.
Answer: B (Daniel Okafor) Okafor: ' perennial crops are much better able to survive droughts and floods than annuals '.
Answer: D (Peter Hale) Hale: ' shoppers can be very reluctant to try unfamiliar grains '.
Answer: A (Helen Marsh) Marsh: ' If we rush new varieties onto the market before they are ready , farmers will be disappointed, and it could set the whole idea back by years.'
Answer: C (Li Wen) Li Wen: the biggest attraction is the labour saved, as ' it is increasingly difficult and expensive to find workers '.
Answer: A (Helen Marsh) Marsh: ' Around two-thirds of the calories people eat come from just a handful of annual grain crops '.
Answer: fertiliser Section B: 'much of the fertiliser applied to fields is washed into rivers'.
Answer: wheat Section C: 'a field of Kernza produces only about a quarter as much grain as a field of wheat '.
Answer: transplanting Section D: 'the backbreaking job of transplanting young rice plants by hand every season'.

text.en: praise the work of certain inventors.
compare two different theories of history.
prove that a popular story is untrue.
describe a widely held belief.

questions.explanation: Answer: D The paragraph presents Carlyle's idea and says ' his view remains remarkably popular ', describing the typical lone-genius story. The writers only criticise it in paragraph 2.

text.en: criticising a point of view
explaining their research methods
summarising the history of an idea
admitting a weakness in their argument

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' We believe that this picture is not simply incomplete but seriously misleading. '

text.en: Their achievements are an exception to the writers' argument.
They depended on the work of earlier artists.
Their importance has been exaggerated.
They should be studied in the same way as scientists.

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' Works of art are, in an important sense, unique to their creators. But science and technology... work very differently.'

text.en: made him more famous than his rivals.
was not appreciated until after his death.
was developed at the same time as a similar one elsewhere.
led to a long legal dispute.

questions.explanation: Answer: C Swan demonstrated bulbs ' at the same time as Edison was developing his own design in the United States '. They formed a joint company rather than going to court (D).

text.en: the simple reason why it was not developed further
the skill with which the toys were made
the length of time it took archaeologists to find it
the influence it had on later inventions

questions.explanation: Answer: A Wheels were never used for transport. ' The explanation is simple: there were no horses, oxen or other large animals to pull carts. '
Answer: NO 'The word genius, in our view, explains nothing.' ' It tells us nothing about how he did so '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writers describe Spencer's argument but say nothing about how other writers received it.
Answer: YES ' Every individual, Spencer insisted, is the product of the time and place in which he or she lives. '
Answer: NO ' it may never be possible to predict the next great breakthrough or the person who will make it '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writers criticise the Nobel Prize rules, but say nothing about what universities are doing.
Answer: F (inspiration) ' The typical story involves a sudden flash of inspiration '.

Answer: D (coincidence) Simultaneous discoveries look like coincidences (' Such coincidences are far more common than most people realise '), but the writers explain them by earlier work, so they are not pure coincidence.
Answer: B (foundations) ' Our answer is that every invention depends on earlier ones. ' The light bulb needed vacuum pumps, electricity and filaments.
Answer: E (accidents) ' Chance also plays a part. ' Fleming's mould, but 'chance favours only the prepared mind'.
